He notes the current inflation is supply-driven (rising oil prices from the Gulf conflict) and argues it need not feed through to wage inflation as it did post-Ukraine in 2022. Labour market conditions are weaker this time — vacancies are falling, private-sector wage growth is only around 2.8%, and workers lack bargaining power. Furthermore, higher energy costs act as a deflationary force longer-term by squeezing consumer spending and reducing corporate pricing power, which could mean fewer rate rises than markets currently price in.

And the other argument that you can make about this external shock, this oil price shock, oil prices going up, fuel prices going up, electricity heating costs going up, in the short term that might push the inflation rate higher. But longer term, that might actually be a deflationary impulse, because people have got less money to spend. Their spending less means companies have less pricing power, they're less profitable, they're probably hiring fewer people. headline: Fidelity's Tom Stevenson explains why tracker mortgages are cheaper than fixed rates, signalling market expectations of UK rate rises
reasoning: Tom Stevenson explains that when variable/tracker mortgage rates are lower than fixed rates, it reflects the market pricing in future rate increases. Lenders offer cheaper variable rates because the interest-rate risk is borne by the borrower; for fixed rates, the lender prices in expected average rates over the fix period to protect against adverse moves. The current spread — with fixed rates spiking above 5% in 2026 while trackers remain around 4% — reflects market expectations that the Bank of England base rate will rise from 3.75% toward 4.5% over the next year or so, driven mainly by oil-price-related inflation following conflict in Iran.

headline: Fidelity's Slingo outlines when to preserve ISA vs pension for inheritance: depends on relative income tax bands of giver and beneficiary
reasoning: Following the April 2027 IHT changes, the decision about which account to draw down first in retirement—if the goal is to maximise inheritance—depends critically on the income tax band of the beneficiary relative to the retiree. If the beneficiary's income tax rate is lower than the retiree's, preserving the pension is still preferable. If the beneficiary pays a higher rate of income tax than the retiree, preserving the ISA is better because inherited ISAs are not subject to income tax. A higher-rate taxpayer beneficiary receiving a pension would face both 40% IHT and 40% income tax, leaving them with only £4,500 on a notional £12,500 pension pot versus £6,000 from an equivalent ISA.
quote: The general rule you have to be thinking about is, is there a difference in the tax bans between the person who is going to be passing on the money and the person who is inheriting that money? And if there is, you have to be very careful about whether you're spending your pension first or your ISA first. So it depends heavily on circumstances. But as a general rule of thumb, you can think that you want to preserve your pension if your child's income tax band is lower than your income tax band. But you will want to preserve your ISA if your child's income tax band is higher than your own income tax band.
episode_title: Pensions & IHT: where to take your retirement money from first

headline: Fidelity's Gemma Slingo warns UK pension savers to review retirement drawdown strategy ahead of April 2027 IHT changes affecting pensions
reasoning: From April next year (2027), UK pensions will become subject to inheritance tax (IHT) for the first time, fundamentally changing the equation of which retirement pot to draw from first. Previously, pensions were IHT-exempt, making them the preferred vehicle to preserve and pass on to beneficiaries. Under new rules, inherited pensions may face a double tax hit: 40% IHT followed by income tax of 20–45% depending on the beneficiary's tax band (if the deceased was over 75). Slingo notes that despite this change, pensions broadly remain the most tax-efficient savings vehicle across their full lifecycle due to contribution tax relief and the 25% tax-free lump sum. headline: AI-related workforce redundancies likely to be slower than feared due to J-curve investment dynamics, limiting near-term impact on ASX earnings
reasoning: Sam Heathersay argues that fears of mass AI-driven redundancies were overinflated, largely promoted by AI startups with vested interests. Companies must invest heavily upfront — in data sets, teams, and retraining — before realising efficiency gains, creating a J-curve effect that delays cost savings. At an aggregate level, companies often hire ahead of AI implementation before eventually reducing headcount. Additionally, disruptive technologies historically make it easier to forecast jobs lost than jobs created, so redundancy projections are naturally skewed negative. For the ASX 200, this means significant workforce disruption is likely to be slower than headline forecasts suggest.
quote: I think there's perhaps some overinflated forecasts of the potential redundancies that we may see as a result of AI. And a lot of them are offered by those that stand to gain the most in AI startups. What we recognize when we speak to companies directly about this point is that there is a level of investment that is required before they can realize the efficiencies on the other side of AI. And it's what we would term the J-curve effect where essentially you have to invest in the foundational data sets, in the teams themselves, in retraining yourself... All of this is naturally inefficient to begin with before you recognize those efficiencies on the other side.

The framework really centered around a number of different factors, but digital vulnerability, one of them task commoditization, as well as focusing on moats, so protection against an AI native startup, whether it's regulatory, proprietary data, integration and customer workflow. headline: Fidelity's Marianna Hunt argues market timing consistently destroys returns relative to staying invested, with 25-year data showing dramatic underperformance for investors who pause contributions during downturns.
reasoning: Hunt constructed a 25-year hypothetical (2000–2025) with three investor personas each contributing £100/month (£31,300 total). 'Calm Carry', who invested continuously regardless of market conditions, ended with ~£158,000. 'Nervous Nora', who moved to cash during falling markets and left it there, ended with ~£108,000 — roughly £50,000 less. 'Yo-Yo Yasmin', who accumulated cash during falls and reinvested in lump sums once markets rose, fared worst at ~£71,000 — nearly £90,000 less than Carry. The key insight is that lump-sum re-entry after a recovery means buying at relatively higher prices and missing the sharpest early-recovery days, which often follow the worst market days. Hunt concludes that automating regular investment contributions is the most effective antidote to timing temptation.
quote: So our first investor was Calm Carry, who invests her 100 pounds a month into the stock market, regardless of what it's doing. Then we had Nervous Nora, who would stop investing her 100 pounds a month when stock markets were falling. Those months, she would put it into cash instead and leave it there, only restarting investing when markets started rising again. And finally, we had Yo-Yo Yasmin. So Yasmin, like Nora, would stop investing when markets were falling. But unlike Nora, she wouldn't leave it in cash permanently. When markets started rising again, she would invest all of the cash that she'd accumulated in a lump sum... She ended up with around 71,000 pounds, which is almost 90,000 pounds worse than Carrie. So you can see there are these big differences that ultimately come down to not how much they were contributing each month, but their behavior.
episode_title: Can you time the market? Here’s what happened when we tried

headline: Hunt warns that behavioural biases — particularly loss aversion — cause investors to over-weight downside risks and underweight the cost of missing strong early-recovery rallies.
reasoning: Hunt draws on behavioural finance to explain why investors repeatedly time the market poorly: the pain of losing money is felt far more acutely than the equivalent gain, causing investors to fixate on avoiding a 20% drawdown while discounting the possibility of missing an equivalent or greater rally while sitting in cash. She also emphasises that the best stock market days frequently follow the worst days, meaning that investors who exit during stress and re-enter after confidence returns systematically miss the sharpest part of recoveries. This psychological dynamic is the root cause of Yo-Yo Yasmin's worst-case outcome in the modelling.
quote: Behavioral finance shows us that the pain of losing money is often far greater to us than the comparable joy of gaining money. So the prospect of losing 20% of your portfolio generally looms much larger than the prospect of potentially gaining an extra 20%. And that means we can fixate on this idea of we don't want to lose money and overlook other risks, which are the risks that A, we could miss out on in investing when prices are cheaper, and B, we could, as you say, miss out on that recovery, which is often quite short and sharp. And then suddenly you're finding that prices are higher than they were before.
episode_title: Can you time the market? Here’s what happened when we tried

headline: Investors at any given moment can find plentiful reasons to avoid investing, but history shows staying invested through uncertainty has consistently rewarded long-term holders
reasoning: Hunt notes that current macro concerns — inflation, interest rates, government debt, geopolitics, and stretched valuations — are especially numerous but are always present in some form. Looking back over the past 25 years, she found a credible reason not to invest in every single year, including the 2018–19 US-China trade war, the 2015 China stock market crash, and the early Covid-19 pandemic. Yet investors who stayed the course through all of these episodes would today be very satisfied. The lesson is that the long-term upward trend in markets is less headline-grabbing than near-term risks, making the temptation to sit on the sidelines persistently hard to resist.
quote: So if we look back at the past kind of 10 to 15 years, a lot of people would say this has been a really good time to be investor. We've had some really strong market performance. But that glosses over the fact that there were specific moments during that time where things were really uncertain and that ultimate outperformance was not clear... I actually found a good reason not to invest for every single one of the past 25 years. But the thing is, if you had invested and kept your money in the market until today, you'd probably be very happy that you did so. So you can see that if you're constantly waiting for what feels like the right time, the safe time, you'll be waiting for a very long time, maybe forever.
